title: Patient Recruitment Knowledge Check: Journey, Funnel, Outreach, Sites and Go-Live

option_rationales: Incorrect. Identification is only the first phase; the solution continues through qualification and handover.
Correct. Identification, qualification and warm handover are the three named phases.
Incorrect. Sites own clinical evaluation, consent and selection - that is where handover lands, not where ClairLabs stops early.
Incorrect. Recruitment is the end of the scope, not site management.
options: Finding participants and stopping at first contact
Identifying participants, qualifying them, and handing them over warm to sites
Running the site's clinical evaluation and consent procedures
Managing trial sites through to study close
questions.prompt: ClairLabs responsibility for a participant ends when the participant is officially selected and recruited. Which three phases does ClairLabs own before that point?
questions.rationale: The deck defines the scope as participant identification, qualification and warm handover, ending once site-specific evaluation clears and the participant is recruited.

option_rationales: Incorrect. The online screener with contact details and initial consent is step 1, primary digital screening.
Incorrect. Platform onboarding of qualified leads is step 2.
Correct. Secondary human screening is step 3: RNN personnel connect, secure consent and run the detailed questionnaire.
Incorrect. Site referral and evaluation is step 4.
options: Primary digital screening
Platform onboarding
Secondary human screening
Site referral and evaluation
questions.prompt: A participant has cleared the online screener and been onboarded to the platform. RNN personnel now connect with them to secure consent and run a detailed questionnaire. Which journey step is this?
questions.rationale: RNN-led consent and detailed questionnaire is secondary human screening, the third step after digital screening and platform onboarding.

option_rationales: Correct. All six appear on the challenges slide: digital outreach, HCP outreach, data-driven outreach, advocacy groups, site alignment with go-live, and patient experience.
Incorrect. There is no investigator-payments pillar; investigator engagement sits under site alignment.
Incorrect. Wearables are one data source, not a standalone pillar.
Incorrect. Site referral speed is a proof point of the patient-centric architecture, not a pillar.
options: Precise digital patient outreach, HCP outreach, data-driven outreach, patient advocacy groups, swift site alignment and go-live, enriched patient experience
Digital outreach, KOL payments, site construction, concierge travel, wearable subsidies, registry buyouts
Six paid-media channels with no site or experience component
Faster site referral, shorter questionnaires, larger call centers, more emails, more sites, more ads
questions.prompt: Which six pillars does the approach use to address patient recruitment challenges?
questions.rationale: The deck names exactly six parallel pillars covering outreach, advocates, sites and experience.

citations.title: Digital technologies used in clinical trial recruitment and enrollment including application to trial diversity and inclusion

option_rationales: Incorrect. Endemic sites like WebMD and Healthline belong to multichannel awareness at the top.
Incorrect. YouTube and programmatic display build top and mid-funnel consideration.
Incorrect. Lead forms, pre-screening tools and search ads are the bottom-funnel close.
Correct. 70-90% initial non-conversion is why re-engagement and retargeting are structural.
options: Awareness is unnecessary because search captures everyone
Consideration is skipped to shorten the funnel
Retargeting is optional and used only for rare diseases
Most people do not convert on first touch, so retargeting runs throughout
questions.prompt: The deck states that 70-90% of people do not convert on first touch. What follows from this for the funnel?
questions.rationale: High initial non-conversion is the stated reason robust re-engagement and retargeting run through the whole funnel.

option_rationales: Incorrect. Geo-fencing medical conferences is a digital-affinity tactic.
Correct. Physician-to-physician trust is named as the primary credibility driver, carried by KOL advocacy through peer networks.
Incorrect. Billboards are offline presence in high-affinity locations.
Incorrect. NPI-targeted programmatic ads are digital affinity.
options: Geo-fencing around medical conferences
KOL advocacy carried by physician-to-physician trust
Billboards near stadiums
NPI-targeted programmatic ads
questions.prompt: Which HCP outreach motion is driven by the deck's stated primary driver of credibility in medical outreach?
questions.rationale: Peer influence - physician-to-physician trust - is the primary credibility driver, and KOL-based influence is the motion built on it.

option_rationales: Incorrect. Wearables contribute behavioral and physiological signals, but the EHR trigger is the embedded-matching one.
Incorrect. Pharmacy networks contribute near-real-time prescription data.
Correct. Trial-matching algorithms are embedded directly in EHRs for immediate identification.
Incorrect. Digital therapeutics platforms contribute verified condition-specific populations.
options: Wearable app ecosystems
Pharmacy network-triggered recruitment
EHR-triggered real-time trial alerts
Digital therapeutics platform populations
questions.prompt: Which intelligence source embeds trial-matching algorithms directly in electronic health records for immediate identification?
questions.rationale: EHR-triggered real-time alerts come from matching algorithms embedded directly within EHRs.

citations.title: Interventions to increase racial and ethnic minority accrual into cancer clinical trials

option_rationales: Incorrect. Advocacy complements site activation; it does not replace it.
Correct. Trust, registries, AI matching and education-led conversion together lift recruitment and cut screen failures.
Incorrect. Media budgets are not a PAG function in the deck.
Incorrect. The 2-day figure is go-live after IRB changes, unrelated to PAGs.
options: Advocacy groups replace the need for site activation
Their trust opens access to hard-to-reach registry populations, AI matching filters precisely, and ambassador-led education cuts misinformation
They fund the media budget for the funnel
They shorten IRB review to two days
questions.prompt: A sponsor asks why advocacy groups matter for a rare-disease trial. What is the strongest deck-grounded answer?
questions.rationale: PAG trust plus registries plus AI inclusion/exclusion matching plus education-led conversion is the deck's advocacy model; IRB timing belongs to the roadmap.

citations.title: Clinical trial enrollment statistics and site performance benchmarks

option_rationales: Incorrect. The model is active: localized outreach plus live monitoring, not passive waiting.
Correct. All five site-alignment elements appear together on the site slide.
Incorrect. Hyper-localized outreach near sites is explicit.
Incorrect. Investigator engagement programmes are a core element.
options: Sign sites and wait for participants to arrive
Rapid activation of high-performing sites, hyper-localized outreach nearby, live performance analytics, investigator engagement and standardized site tools
One national campaign with no local component
Analytics only, with no investigator contact
questions.prompt: Which combination best describes site alignment?
questions.rationale: The deck's site model combines rapid activation, hyper-localized outreach, live analytics, investigator programmes and standardized tools targeted at high patient-density locations.

option_rationales: Incorrect. AI matching is tier 1; confused participants need the human tier.
Correct. Simplifying eligibility, securing consent and detailing the questionnaire is the RNN tier's job.
Incorrect. Referral follows qualification, never skips it.
Incorrect. Confusion is handled by simplification, not by dropping the case.
options: The AI tier re-runs the match and the case closes automatically
RNN personnel simplify the complex eligibility questions, secure consent and run the detailed questionnaire
The participant is referred to the site immediately without screening
The case is dropped as unrecruitable
questions.prompt: A participant is confused by eligibility wording. Under 2-tier smart screening, what happens?
questions.rationale: Tier 2 is human: RNN simplifies complex eligibility questions for patients, secures consent and runs the detailed questionnaire.

option_rationales: Incorrect. Ad optimization is week 6 work, after go-live.
Correct. The roadmap chains week 2 submission and week 3 preparation into the week 4 go-live event.
Incorrect. Training content exists, but the quiz is not a go-live dependency in the deck.
Incorrect. Case numbers are proof material, not schedule dependencies.
options: All advertising must already be fully optimized
Sponsor review and IRB-ready submission completed in week 2, with internal prep, testing and training done in week 3
The 12-question quiz must be passed by all staff
Case-study numbers must be re-verified
questions.prompt: Go-live is planned for week 4. What must be true for that date to hold?
questions.rationale: Week 4 go-live lands within 2 days of IRB changes only if week 2 sponsor/IRB submission and week 3 prep, testing and training complete on schedule.

option_rationales: Incorrect. Case results are not universal guarantees.
Correct. Both figures appear in the deck's success-stories material.
Incorrect. Site referral in minutes describes the architecture's compression, not a guarantee.
Incorrect. The deck claims reduced screen failures, never zero.
options: Every trial everywhere delivers exactly 61% more patients
Cases including 61% more patients delivered and a 12-month recruitment request delivered in 10 months
Guaranteed site referral in under one minute for all trials
Zero screen failures on every programme
questions.prompt: Which outcome figures from the deck's case studies can be quoted in training?
questions.rationale: The deck reports 61% more patients delivered and a 12-month target delivered in 10 months as case outcomes; the escalation rule is to re-verify before quoting externally.

option_rationales: Correct. Real-time feedback loops replace end-of-study surveys.
Incorrect. Real-time engagement platforms add consistent communication; they do not replace the platform.
Incorrect. Peer testimonials build trust but never replace consent.
Incorrect. Journey mapping stays; it identifies the pain points to fix.
options: It replaces end-of-study surveys with real-time feedback loops for immediate improvement
It replaces the platform with phone calls
It replaces consent with testimonials
It replaces journey mapping with larger ad budgets
questions.prompt: What does the patient-centric architecture replace, and with what?
questions.rationale: Continuous feedback loops shift measurement from end-of-study surveys to real-time mechanisms that drive immediate improvement.
